What he says is that the sea does not care who writes it down, and that somebody has to write it.

questions.question: How many lines does Shen Hai write in his record each day?
Why does he keep the oldest book in a drawer and the newest one on the desk?

options.A: Because the drawer is dry and the desk is not.
options.B: Because he wants to finish the newest one first.
options.C: Because a book that is used is hard to read.
options.D: Because the office asks him to keep only one book.

questions.question: About how many lines has he written in the last ten years?
How did the number of the new kind of line change?

options.A: There were eleven new lines last winter.
options.B: There were four new lines this winter and two last winter.
options.C: There were two new lines last winter and none this winter.
options.D: There were two lines two winters ago and four last winter.

questions.question: What does Shen Hai mean by saying that the sea does not care who writes it down?

options.A: Somebody has to write it down, whoever that person is.
options.B: Nobody reads the record, so writing it is a waste of time.
options.C: The boats should write their own names in the book.
options.D: The lamp would work just as well without a keeper.

title: 退休教师的三层花架
material: Ms. Luo taught history for thirty-two years and retired in March. She lives on the sixth floor, and in April she built a shelf of three boards against the balcony rail. The bottom board is for things that can survive being forgotten: two pots of green onion and a bag of soil. The middle board is for her three pots of tomato, and she counts them. The top board is for the cuttings she keeps because a friend gave them to her. She waters at seven, before the sun turns the balcony into a hot plate, and the whole job takes fifteen minutes. Watering at five in the evening would be better for the tomatoes and worse for her back. In her first summer she grew nine tomatoes and gave away seven. In her second she grew five and gave away five, which she says is a better year. She has a note book in which each pot has a page, and on the page she writes only two things: the date it was planted and whether it fruited. She stopped writing about watering in June of the first year, because she had been doing the same thing every morning for a hundred days and had nothing new to say.

questions.question: What does Ms. Luo put on the bottom board?

options.B: The cuttings that a friend gave her.
options.C: Nothing at all there that needs daily care.
options.D: Two green-onion pots and a bag of soil.

questions.question: Why does she water at seven in the morning rather than at five in the evening?

options.A: Because the office building is closed in the evening.
options.B: Because evening water suits the tomatoes but not her back.
options.C: Because the tomato leaves burn in the evening sun.
options.D: Because her friend waters the balcony for her in the evening.

questions.question: Why did she stop writing about watering in June of the first year?

options.A: Because her note book filled up that June.
options.B: Because she gave the note book back to her friend.
options.C: Because she did the same thing for a hundred days.
options.D: Because the green onion in the bottom board died in June.

questions.question: In which summer did she give away all the tomatoes she grew?
What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: Why tomatoes are hard to grow on a sixth-floor balcony.
options.B: What a retired history teacher does with a gift from a friend.
options.C: How many tomatoes one family can grow in a summer.
options.D: How a retired teacher keeps three boards going on a balcony.

title: 只开三个月的渡船
material: The ferry at Shuangzhou runs from the first of May to the last of July and not one day more. The skipper is a man of fifty-eight called Lu Ming, and he has made the crossing eleven thousand times in twenty-two years. In the other nine months the boat lies at the north bank under a cover of blue tarpaulin, and Lu Ming works on engines at a garage in the county town. The crossing takes thirty-five minutes each way and the fare is fifteen yuan. In those three months the ferry carries about four thousand people, which is a good year; a bad one is two thousand. Lu Ming keeps two lists, one for the passengers and one for the freight, and he writes the freight list in pencil because the paper gets wet. His daughter is an accountant in the city and has offered to put the numbers into a computer for him. He has not said yes. When the ferry runs, he writes the time he left and the time he arrived, and at the end of July he turns the page and starts the next year from one again.

questions.question: How long does the ferry run each year?

options.A: All the year round without a single break.
options.B: From the first of May to July.
options.C: From the first of May to September.
options.D: For about eleven months of every year.

questions.question: What does Lu Ming do during the other nine months?

options.A: He works on engines at a garage in the county town.
options.B: He takes passengers over in a small rowing boat.
options.C: He writes lists for the county town office.
options.D: He stays on the north bank beside the boat under a cover.

questions.question: What can we learn about the number of passengers?

options.A: It is always about the same in every year.
options.B: It was about two thousand people in that very last good year.
options.C: A bad year is always about four thousand.
options.D: A good year is about four thousand, a bad one two thousand.

questions.question: Why does Lu Ming write the freight list in pencil?

options.A: Because he has no other pencil.
options.B: Because pencil can be bought in the county town.

questions.question: What does the story of the two lists tell us about Lu Ming?

options.A: That he does not trust his daughter.
options.B: That he keeps his own plain records by hand.
options.C: That the county town asked him to count the freight.
options.D: That the ferry carried four thousand people last May.

title: 裁缝口袋里的小尺子
material: Mr. Liang has a tape measure in his pocket that is not a tape measure. It is a small steel ruler about fifteen centimetres long with a hole in one end, and he has carried it since he opened his shop. The shop takes in clothes that other shops will not touch: coats with strange linings, curtains with a metre of extra cloth sewn into the hem, trousers that belonged to a great-grandfather. People say he looks at a garment for a long time before he says a price, and they are right, but what he is doing is not thinking. He is finding the seam. Once the original seam is visible, the alteration is easy, because the cloth tells you where it was meant to end. He has never thrown away a garment that he could not mend, and he has sent back four to their owners rather than cut them up. His shop opens at nine and shuts at six, and between one and two he eats at the same table as his two apprentices. The ruler cost him nine yuan in 1979 and he says it is the only tool he owns that has never needed to be replaced.

questions.question: What is unusual about the ruler in Mr. Liang's pocket?

options.A: It cannot measure anything longer than fifteen centimetres.
options.B: It was made in 1979 and is therefore very old.
options.C: It is a small steel ruler, not a tape measure.
options.D: He keeps it only for measuring curtains at the shop.

questions.question: What does Mr. Liang do before he tells a customer the price?

options.B: He asks the customer what she paid for it.
options.C: He checks whether the shop can finish the work.

questions.question: Why is the original seam so important to him?

options.A: Because it shows how much the garment cost him.
options.B: Because once the seam is visible the alteration is easy.
options.C: Because every garment that comes into his shop has a visible seam.
options.D: Because his father taught him how to find it.

questions.question: Why did he send four garments back instead of cutting them up?

options.A: Because he never throws away a mendable garment.
options.B: Because his two apprentices refused to do that kind of work.
options.C: Because the shop was closed for four days that week.
options.D: Because the customers came back for them after four days.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: Why a tailor keeps an old steel ruler.
options.B: How curtains are measured before they are cut.
options.C: How one tailor decides what work he can and cannot take.
options.D: What a shop that opens at nine and shuts at six is.

title: 每周三晚上开机的短波电台
material: Han Yu is fourteen and owns a radio that most people in his street cannot switch on. It stood in a cupboard in his grandfather's house for eleven years before he asked to have it. The first thing he learned was that a radio has to be warmed up; the dial only means something after the set has been on for about ten minutes. He now listens on Wednesday evenings, because that is when the station two thousand kilometres away sends its reading at nine. He writes the numbers in a school exercise book, with the date at the top of the page, and by the end of a year the book is full. His grandfather kept the same numbers for eleven years without writing them down, and Han Yu has found four of his pages in a biscuit tin, each with a different date on it. The station is not on every Wednesday; it misses two or three a year, and Han Yu has learned to tell the difference between a station that is off and a set that is broken, because a broken set hums and an off station is silent. He has never told his class why he does this.

questions.question: What is the first thing Han Yu learned about his radio?

options.A: The dial only means something after the set has been on for about ten minutes.
options.B: The set has to be carried outside before it will ever really work at all.
options.C: The station transmits only on Wednesday evenings.
options.D: The dial has to be cleaned every week.

questions.question: How long had the radio been in the cupboard?
Why does Han Yu listen on Wednesday evenings?

options.A: Because his grandfather told him to.
options.B: Because the station two thousand kilometres away sends its reading at nine that evening.
options.C: Because the school exercise book is only really free on Wednesday at all then.
options.D: Because his class meets on Wednesday.

questions.question: How can Han Yu tell that the set is broken rather than the station off?

options.A: The station sends a short notice before it ever stops.
options.B: His grandfather's book has four pages in it.
options.C: The set becomes warmer than usual.
options.D: A broken set hums and an off station is silent.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: How a boy keeps a written record of a radio station that his grandfather also kept.
options.B: Why most people in his street cannot use a radio.
options.C: What really happens to a radio that is just left alone in a cupboard for years.
options.D: How a school exercise book gets full in one year.

title: 修了四十年自行车的老师傅
material: Mr. Dai has repaired bicycles for forty-one years from a stall the size of a small table, and he can name the year of a bicycle from the shape of its chain. He says a bicycle tells you its age before you count anything: the chain gets thin at the pins, the brake blocks get small, and the pedal ends go flat. He charges eight yuan for a full service, which takes about an hour, and he does not charge extra for a bicycle that is old. In his first ten years he fixed about four hundred bicycles a year. Now it is close to a hundred and twenty, and he says that is not because people ride less, but because they ride further. The nearest proper shop is four kilometres away, and a bus to it costs two yuan each way. A boy brought in a bicycle last month and asked whether it was worth repairing. Mr. Dai turned the back wheel, listened to it, and said that the frame was sound and one wheel needed a new spoke; that is forty yuan and twenty minutes, and the boy will keep it for years. The stall has no sign, and Mr. Dai has never put one up.

questions.question: How does Mr. Dai decide how old a bicycle is?

options.A: He counts the scratches on the frame.
options.B: He just asks the owner how long it has really been used.
options.C: He reads the year written on the bell.
options.D: He looks at the chain, the brake blocks and the pedal ends.

questions.question: How much does Mr. Dai charge for a full service?
Why does he say the number of bicycles he repairs has fallen?

options.A: People ride further than they used to, and the nearest proper shop is four kilometres away.
options.B: People ride less than they used to.
options.C: His stall has really no sign at all, so new customers never even really find him.
options.D: Eight yuan is more than it was forty-one years ago.

questions.question: What did Mr. Dai tell the boy about his bicycle last month?

options.A: That the frame was not worth repairing.
options.B: That the whole bicycle needed a new chain.
options.C: That the frame was sound but one wheel needed a new spoke.
options.D: That it would really be much cheaper to buy a new bicycle.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: Why a bicycle gets more expensive as it gets older.
options.B: What a man who has repaired bicycles for forty-one years looks at, and what he charges.
options.C: How far it really is from that stall to the nearest proper shop at all then.
options.D: Why the stall has never had a sign.

title: 只卖三种面包的小店
material: The bakery on Green Street sells three kinds of bread and has done for nineteen years. The owner, Auntie Mo, will not add a fourth, and she has been asked about it so often that she keeps a list of the ones that were refused. They are a cheese loaf, a cake, and a roll with olives in it. Her bread is made once a day, at two in the morning, and there are ninety loaves by six. If any are left at nine they go to the door of the primary school, and if they are still there at eleven they go home with the staff. Nothing is sold on the second day, which surprises people. Green, her assistant, is twenty-three and has worked there for four years. She can tell a customer who has bought the plain loaf every week for two years by the way they look at the shelf first, before they look at her. Auntie Mo says the shop has never sold a thing that was not baked in that building, and that this is the only rule she has. In the second year the queue for the red bean bun reached the corner, and Auntie Mo did not make more than ninety that day either.

questions.question: What does Auntie Mo do with bread that is left at nine?

options.A: She keeps it until the next morning.
options.B: She sells it at a lower price in the afternoon.
options.C: She takes it to the door of the primary school.
options.D: She gives it to the staff at eleven.

questions.question: Why is the bread made at two in the morning?

options.A: So that ninety loaves are ready by six.
options.B: So that the oven is cold enough at midnight.
options.C: So that the staff arrive at six.
options.D: So that school children get it at nine.

questions.question: How can Green tell a customer who has bought the plain loaf every week for two years?

options.A: By the money that the customer ever puts on the shelf at all.
options.B: By the name the customer calls Auntie Mo.
options.C: By the hour the customer comes in.
options.D: By the way the customer looks at the shelf before looking at her.

questions.question: According to Auntie Mo, what is the only rule the shop has?

options.A: Nobody at all may ever buy any bread in the shop after nine.
options.B: The shop never sells a thing that was not baked in that building.
options.C: Bread that is left over is never sold at a lower price.
options.D: There are always ninety loaves a day.

questions.question: What does the passage tell us about the red bean bun?

options.A: It is the kind Auntie Mo refuses to bake, and her bread is made at two in the morning.
options.B: It is the kind that takes longest to make, and her bread is made at two in the morning.
options.C: Auntie Mo has written it on her refused list, and her bread is made at two in the morning.
options.D: It is the kind that brings a queue, but she still did not bake more than ninety that day.

title: 教孩子游泳的老教练
material: Coach Xie taught at the town pool for thirty-six years and never learned to swim well himself, because a coach in that pool only ever taught the shallow end. He knows nine children who can float at three, and he can tell from the way they stand at the edge which ones will. The rule in his pool is that a child is never held by the arms; a child is held under the chest, so that the arms stay free. He taught four hundred and sixty children in his first ten years and a hundred and thirty in his last ten. The reason is not that the pool closed, because the pool was open all ten years, but that more of the children came with an adult on each side. He still keeps the paper list from his first year. Forty names on it are written in a hand that is not his, because the first year he wrote down the names of children who could not yet swim and one of the mothers filled them in. He says a list is only useful if you can still read it.

questions.question: Why did Coach Xie never learn to swim well himself?

options.A: Because the pool there was really too shallow just near the door.
options.B: Because a coach in that pool only ever taught the shallow end.
options.C: Because he was afraid of the deep water.
options.D: Because he never went to the pool himself.

questions.question: How is a child held in the water in his pool?

options.B: By just one arm only, at the shallow end.
options.D: Under the chest, so that the arms stay free.

questions.question: Why does he teach far fewer children now than in his first ten years?

options.A: Because the pool closed for ten years.
options.B: Because there are really far fewer children left in the town these days.
options.C: Because more of the children now come with an adult on each side.
options.D: Because he stopped keeping the paper list.

questions.question: Why are forty names on his first-year list not in his handwriting?

options.A: Because the mothers of children who could not yet swim filled them in.
options.B: Because a student from his own class wrote them all down for him.
options.C: Because the list was bought second-hand.
options.D: Because he wrote the list out twice.

questions.question: What does he mean by saying that a list is only useful if you can still read it?

options.A: He thinks the old list should be thrown away.
options.B: He means the old paper from that first year has really all faded away.
options.C: He means the names are worth keeping only while they can still be used.
options.D: He means the list is now too long to keep.

title: 用废木头做玩具车的老人
material: Uncle Bai began making toy cars out of wood boxes in the spring of last year, when a shop on his street gave away its packing cases. He uses the flat sides, cuts a wheel from the corner where the wood is strongest, and nails four on. A car takes him about forty minutes and holds three children on its floor, which he thinks is enough. He made seventy-four last year and gave sixty-one away. The other thirteen are on a shelf in the community room, and a child may take one and leave it there for the next one. He keeps the list of who brought the box and what the car is worth to him, which is nothing, though it cost him about six yuan in nails. His rule is that a child must be able to reach the floor, so the height is fixed and he will not change it for anybody. Last winter he made eighteen in a month when he was not well, and he says that he would not do it again, and that he has already started eleven this month.

questions.question: Where does Uncle Bai get the wood for the cars?

options.A: From packing cases that a shop gives away.
options.B: From a timber yard just near the market.
options.C: From the shelf in the community room.

questions.question: About how long does one toy car take him?
How many cars did he give away last year?
Why does he fix the height of the car and refuse to change it?

options.A: Because the nails are too short for a taller car.
options.B: Because a taller car needs more wood.
options.C: Because a child must be able to reach the floor.
options.D: Because the shop does not give away large cases.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: How one old man makes toy cars out of thrown-away packing cases.
options.B: Why the community room keeps a shelf of toy cars.
options.C: What Uncle Bai does in the winter when he is not well.
options.D: How much wood one toy car needs.

title: 一天走四十里的送货员
material: Old Chen delivers bread and cakes to forty-two shops in the town, and he does it on foot because there is no room in the van for a bicycle as well. He starts at three in the morning at the bakery and finishes by ten. The round is about twenty kilometres, and on a hot day he has to stop three times. He carries two bags, one for cakes and one for bread, and the cakes go in first because they are light and nothing can be put under them in the other bag. He has done this for twenty-six years and knows which shops will be open and which will still be shut at four. He does not knock at the back door of any shop; he leaves the bag in the gap by the door and writes the time on the top of it. If he finds the bag still there on the way back, he knows it was not taken. Last month he wrote a new time on the same bag six times in one morning because the door of that shop was blocked by a delivery of paint, and he says that he never complains about it, because a shop that cannot open is not his business.

questions.question: Why does Old Chen deliver on foot?

options.A: Because the van is really used for other work in the early morning.
options.B: Because the town is too small for a van.
options.C: Because there is no room in the van for a bicycle as well.
options.D: Because all the shops are within walking distance of one another.

questions.question: Why do the cakes go in the first bag?

options.A: Because the first bag is the larger one, and he carries two bags on foot.
options.B: Because the shops sell more bread than cakes, and he carries two bags on foot.
options.C: Because the bread is delivered at four, and he does the whole round on foot.
options.D: Because they are light and nothing can be put under them in the other bag.

questions.question: How can Old Chen tell that a shop has taken a bag?

options.A: Because the bag is not there when he comes back.
options.B: Because the shopkeeper thanks him at the door.
options.C: Because he sees the shopkeeper through the glass.
options.D: Because the time he wrote on it is really different.

questions.question: What happened outside the shop whose door was blocked by paint?

options.A: Old Chen really left the bag in the gap by the door as usual.
options.B: He wrote a new time on the same bag six times in one morning.
options.C: He walked the whole round a second time.
options.D: He complained to the shopkeeper about the paint.

questions.question: What does the passage tell us about the last shop in his round?

options.A: That it is really the only shop in the town that he does not deliver to.
options.B: That it is the shop he complains about most.
options.C: That it is the nearest one to the bakery.
options.D: That its being unable to open early is a matter for the shop, not for him.

title: 山里的护林员
material: Wei Ming has walked the same eleven kilometres of fire line for twenty-two years, and he knows it by the shape rather than by the map. He goes up in the last week of March, when the ground is still hard, and comes down in the second week of November, before the snow. In between he has a bicycle and a small tent, and he sleeps in the hut on the fourth kilometre most weeks. The hut has a stove and a bed and a window that looks south, and he has painted the window frame twice. He does not go up on a day when there is no need; the station in the village rings him if a column of smoke is seen from the road. In twenty-two years the station has rung nine times, and seven of those were cooking fires on a farm. He keeps a list of the dates and the wind direction, and he reads the list before he goes up each year. The list is his own and nobody has ever asked to see it. He says the best week is the last one, in November, because the trees are bare and a fire can be seen from a very long way off.

questions.question: For how long does Wei Ming stay on the mountain each year?

options.B: From the last week of March to the first week of November.
options.C: From the last week of March to the second week of November.
options.D: From the second week of November to the last week of March.

questions.question: Why does he come down in November?

options.A: Because the ground is hard in March and the snow comes in November.
options.B: Because the station rings him in November.
options.C: Because the window of the little hut really does look south that way.
options.D: Because the trees are bare in November.

questions.question: What can we learn about the nine times the station has rung?

options.A: Seven of them were real fires in the forest that anyone could see for miles.
options.B: Two of them were cooking fires on a farm.
options.C: Each ring led to a new column of smoke.
options.D: Most were not forest fires; seven of the nine were cooking fires on a farm.

questions.question: What does he do with the list of dates and wind directions?

options.A: He gives a copy to the village station every year.
options.B: He reads it before he goes up each year.
options.C: He pins it to the wall of the hut.
options.D: He hands it over when he retires.

questions.question: Why does he call the last week the best one?

options.A: Because he has no work to do then, and the window frame has already been painted twice.
options.B: Because the hut has just been painted, and he sleeps in the hut on the fourth kilometre.
options.C: Because the snow has not come yet, and the wind direction is on the list he reads.
options.D: Because the trees are bare and a fire can be seen from a very long way off.

title: 印刷厂里写春联的师傅
material: Mr. Xu has written the red paper for the door of his street since he was twenty-six, and the shop has printed the rest. A pair is written twice: once in the morning, in a hard pencil, and once in the afternoon, in ink, when the paper has dried. He writes the fourteen characters of a long pair, and the small pair is nine. Ink is expensive, so the first attempt is made in pencil and only the good one is inked; about two in five of the long pairs are thrown away. The paper comes from a warehouse four streets away and is cut on a Friday. He keeps every one of the first characters in a box, sorted by shape, because the first character is what people stop at. In fifty years he has written about nine thousand pairs. He can no longer write the brush character for wind, and he says he does not mind, because people do not look at the fourth character from the left; they look at the first one. Two years ago the printing shop asked him to train a boy. The boy left after four months.

questions.question: Why is the first attempt made in pencil?

options.A: Because the shop has no red ink.
options.B: Because ink is expensive, so only the good one is inked.
options.C: Because the paper is really only ever cut on a Friday.
options.D: Because the boy cannot use a brush.

questions.question: Why does Mr. Xu keep the first characters in a box?

options.A: Because the printing shop really needs them all for its type.
options.B: Because the character for wind is the hardest one.
options.C: Because he wants to give them away.
options.D: Because the first character is the one people stop at.

questions.question: How many characters are there in a long pair of red paper?
What happened when the shop asked him to train a boy two years ago?

options.A: The boy stayed for four years.
options.B: The boy would not learn to write in pencil.
options.C: The boy left after four months.
options.D: The shop gave up the idea of training anyone.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: Why red paper is only ever cut on a Friday at a warehouse four streets away.
options.B: How one man has written the door paper of his street for fifty years.
options.C: What the two different inks used in one day are.
options.D: Why people do not look at the fourth character.

title: 周末才开门的修理铺
material: The repair shop on Pine Street opens on Saturday and Sunday only, and has done for twenty-nine years. Zhou Bing, who runs it, is seventy-one. He was a factory mechanic for thirty-two years and he took the week off on Friday nights, which is when he did the repairs that could not wait: a kettle lead, a lamp plug, a chair leg. When the factory closed he kept only that day. He fixes four things a week, and there is no charge for the first half hour of looking at a thing. He keeps a tin of parts behind the counter and about a third of the jobs end with him using something from that tin. People bring him things from three towns, because the shop next door with a proper counter does not open at all in August. He says a job that is not finished in an hour is not his job, and he sends those to the shop with the counter. His hands are slow now. A kettle takes him forty minutes; it took him twenty-five when he was fifty.

questions.question: Why did Zhou Bing keep Friday night after the factory closed?

options.A: Because the shop next door opens on Friday, and it has opened for twenty-nine years.
options.B: Because his hands are slow, and a kettle takes him forty minutes instead of twenty-five.
options.C: Because the factory asked him to, and he was a factory mechanic for thirty-two years.
options.D: Because Friday night was the day he had always done repairs that could not wait.

questions.question: How many things does he fix in a week?
Why do people bring him things from three towns?

options.A: Because his shop opens at the weekend and the shop next door does not open at all in August.
options.B: Because the tin behind his counter has more parts, and about a third of his jobs end that way.
options.C: Because his prices are lower than any other shop, and he has no charge for the first half hour.
options.D: Because the factory used to send its own workers to him, and he was a mechanic for thirty-two years.

questions.question: What does he do with a job that is not finished in an hour?

options.A: He sends it to the shop with the counter.
options.B: He keeps it until the next Saturday.
options.C: He charges for the first half hour only.
options.D: He asks the customer to come back in August.

questions.question: What does the passage tell us about Zhou Bing's hands?

options.A: They were always slow, even when he was fifty.
options.B: They are no longer able to hold a tool.
options.C: A kettle takes him forty minutes now, and twenty-five when he was fifty.
options.D: They are really the reason he now works only four jobs a week.

title: 给字典编例句的中学生
material: Lin Yu is sixteen and has written an example sentence for every word in one dictionary, from the first page to the last. She started in September with a rule: a sentence must be one she has actually said out loud, and it must not need a dictionary of its own. The dictionary has about eighteen thousand head words and eleven hundred of them are names of things she has never seen. For those she leaves the line empty and writes the page number instead, so she can come back. Her English teacher said the work was a waste of paper and then, in January, set the same task for a class of forty. Twenty-six of them finished. She does not write in the margins, because a dictionary with more words in it is harder to use, not easier. She keeps the finished pages in order in a box file, and she has used her own sentences more than once when she has forgotten a word. She says the dictionary was not written for her and she is writing her own.

questions.question: What rule did Lin Yu start with in September?

options.A: A sentence must be one she has actually said out loud and must not need a dictionary of its own.
options.B: Every head word must have a sentence, with no exceptions at all, and she keeps the finished pages in order.
options.C: Sentences must be written in the margins, and she keeps all the finished pages in order in a box file.
options.D: Sentences must be at least ten words long, and she began all of this herself in September with a rule.

questions.question: What does she do with a head word for a thing she has never seen?

options.A: She invents a sentence for it.
options.B: She leaves the line empty and writes the page number.
options.D: She copies the whole sentence straight out of another dictionary.

questions.question: Why does she not write in the margins?

options.A: Because the margins are too narrow, and her own box file would not shut.
options.B: Because her teacher told her not to, and she keeps her own sentences anyway.
options.C: Because a dictionary with more words in it is harder to use, not easier.
options.D: Because the pages would no longer close, and she keeps the pages in order.

questions.question: What happened after her English teacher set the same task for the class?

options.B: Her teacher stopped the exercise in January.
options.C: Only Lin Yu's pages were kept.
options.D: Twenty-six of the forty finished it.

questions.question: What does she mean by saying that the dictionary was not written for her?

options.A: She is writing a set of examples that she can use herself.
options.B: She only thinks that the dictionary has far too many head words.
options.C: She cannot read the print in the dictionary.
options.D: She wants a different dictionary for the class.

title: 在屋顶上孵蛋的母鸡
material: The hen on the roof of the building at number 9 has laid fourteen eggs in two years, and nobody in the block can say who owns her. She came there in the way such birds come, which is that nobody is looking, and she has stayed on the flat top of the stair well ever since. Her eggs are not all in one place; she moves them. In March she was on the water tank, in June she was behind the pipe, and in November she was in the corner by the door where the sun comes first. On the first cold morning she covers them and uncovers them the next day, which is more than most people manage with a single egg. She has raised four young from the fourteen. The block has asked the council twice about her and been told twice that she is not a nuisance. Auntie Guo, who lives on the third floor and cannot climb, has a folding chair carried up for her once a week in the warm months, and she goes up in her brother's lift.

questions.question: How many eggs has the hen laid in two years?
Why are the eggs not all in one place?

options.A: Because the block keeps moving her.
options.B: Because the sun damages them in one spot.
options.C: Because the council asked her to move them.

questions.question: What happens on the first cold morning?

options.B: She covers the eggs and uncovers them the next day.
options.C: She really moves to the corner by the door that gets the sun.
options.D: Auntie Guo carries her a chair.

questions.question: What has the council said about the hen?

options.A: Twice that she is not a nuisance.
options.B: The council said once that she must be moved.
options.D: That Auntie Guo may keep her.

questions.question: What does the passage tell us about Auntie Guo?

options.A: That she lives on the top floor, and she goes up in her brother's lift once a week too.
options.B: That a chair is carried up for her twice a week, and she carries it up herself in winter.
options.C: That she cannot climb, and a chair is carried up for her once a week in the warm months.
options.D: That she takes the eggs away each week, and the corner by the door is where the sun comes.

title: 存了三十年邮票的看门人
material: Uncle Hong has been the gatekeeper at the middle school since he left it as a boy, and for thirty years he collected stamps in the pocket book he carried on the night rounds. He never bought a rare one. He says a rare stamp needs money and he never had money, but a stamp that has been through a school is free and there are more of those than people think. He has about eleven thousand, in nine pocket books, and they are all ordinary: festivals, cities, birds, and a great many with a postmark nobody can read. Once a year, in the last week of August, he puts the books on the desk in the duty room and the children may look, but nobody may take one. Eleven years ago a boy slipped one into his pocket and Uncle Hong said nothing to him and said nothing to the boy's father, and the boy came back three weeks later with it. In his last year at the gate he gave the whole lot to the school library in a box, and asked for one thing: that they be kept in the order he had them in.

questions.question: Why did Uncle Hong never buy a rare stamp?

options.A: Because he never really knew what a rare stamp was at all.
options.B: Because a rare stamp needs money and he never had money.
options.C: Because his pocket books were already full.

questions.question: Where did most of his stamps come from?

options.A: From school post that came free.
options.B: From an ordinary little shop somewhere in the city.

questions.question: What happened eleven years ago?

options.A: A boy was then really caught taking a whole little pocket book of old stamps.
options.B: The boy's father came to the gate.
options.C: A boy slipped a stamp into his pocket and gave it back three weeks later.
options.D: The children asked to keep the stamps.

questions.question: When may the children look at the books?

options.A: Every evening after the last round.
options.B: At any time, but they may not take one.
options.C: Only really in the last week of the middle school year.
options.D: In the last week of August, and nobody may take one.

questions.question: What did he ask for when he gave the stamps to the library?

options.A: That they be kept in the order he had them in.
options.B: That the library buy a new box.
options.C: That his own name be put right on all the books.
options.D: That the children may take them.

title: 冬天推车卖烤红薯
material: Uncle Yan pushes a cart of roast sweet potatoes into the market square daily from the tenth of November to the tenth of February, and no day before or after. He buys them eighty kilometres away at four yuan a kilo and sells them at six, so a good day is about thirty kilos and a bad one fifteen. He says the bad ones are the warm days, when people still want ice, not something hot. The oven under the cart holds six kilos at a time and takes fifty minutes, so he can turn over a batch every hour from three in the afternoon. The square is closed to carts on Sunday morning, and that is when he washes the cart, which costs him an hour he does not lose, since he is not there anyway. He keeps the burnt ones for himself and gives them to the man who moves the bins; he does not sell them at a lower price. He has pushed the same cart for nineteen years and has never once been late, not even when snow closed the road in the first week. He says what has really cost him is his left knee, and he blames the slope at the north end of the square rather than the cold.

questions.question: How long does Uncle Yan sell sweet potatoes in the square?

options.B: From the tenth of February to the tenth of November.
options.C: From the tenth of November to the tenth of March.
options.D: From the tenth of November to the tenth of February.

questions.question: What makes a day bad for him?

options.A: When the price of sweet potatoes rises in the far town.
options.B: When the weather is warm and people still want ice.
options.C: When the square is closed to carts.
options.D: When the man who moves the bins does not come.

questions.question: How much can the oven under the cart hold at one time?
Why does he wash the cart on Sunday morning?

options.A: Because the square is closed to carts then.
options.B: Because the sweet potatoes are sold faster on Sunday.
options.C: Because the oven is cleaner on Sunday.
options.D: Because the man who moves the bins comes then.

questions.question: What does he blame for his left knee?

options.A: The snow that closed the road in the first week of that year.
options.B: The slope at the north end of the square rather than the cold.
options.C: Nineteen years of pushing the same cart every week.
options.D: The oven under the cart, which takes fifty minutes for each batch.

title: 教盲人用手机的志愿者
material: Mr. Pei is seventy-eight and teaches four people to use a mobile phone, and he learned all of it after he lost his sight. That is the whole of his qualification, and he says it out loud before anybody asks. The four are all over sixty and none of them wanted to be taught by their own children. The lesson is ninety minutes and it never changes: find the phone, find the volume button, ring one number, stop. Anything else is a second lesson, and there have been eleven second lessons. He keeps the phones in a box with the numbers written on the outside in large print, because the phones themselves are all different. His own phone has no case, since he cannot feel a case anyway. He says the hardest part is not the buttons; it is that a blind person cannot see a stranger's face turn away when they cannot help. In the fourth year one of his four wrote a number into his hand at the end of the lesson, and Mr. Pei asked whether it was a telephone or a taxi, and both of them laughed for a while.

questions.question: Why does Mr. Pei say he is the right person to teach this?

options.A: Because he lost his sight and had to learn to use a phone.
options.B: Because he worked in a telephone office for forty years before all this.
options.C: Because he has read about phones in a newspaper.
options.D: Because his own children use phones every day.

questions.question: What happens in a second lesson?

options.A: He teaches the same four steps again.
options.B: The students bring a relative with them.
options.C: Something is taught that is not one of the four steps.
options.D: He explains what a phone is for, before the lesson starts.

questions.question: Why does he keep the phones in a box with large numbers on the outside?

options.A: Because the box keeps all the phones safe and sound.
options.B: Because the students cannot feel the numbers on them.
options.C: Because the phones have different buttons on them, in different places on every single one.
options.D: Because the phones are all different and the students cannot tell them apart by touch.

questions.question: Why does he say the hardest part is not the buttons?

options.A: Because the buttons are in a language he cannot read.
options.B: Because a blind person cannot see a stranger's face turn away.
options.C: Because the phone is too heavy to hold for a long time.
options.D: Because his students forget the four steps.

questions.question: What does the passage tell us about the four people he teaches?

options.A: They are all over sixty and none of them wanted to be taught by their own children.
options.B: They all work in the same office.

title: 每年只画一幅画的老人
material: Mr. Deng painted one picture a year for thirty-one years, and he has kept every one of them. They are small, about the size of a sheet of paper, and they are all of the same street seen from the same window. One a year was not a rule he set; it was what the calendar allowed, because he paints in the first week of January when the light is flat. In 2009 he painted nothing at all, and the gap is the only one. He says the year without a picture was the year he stopped speaking to his brother, and that the painting had nothing to do with it, though he can understand why people think it does. When a student from the college asked to see the pictures, he showed her four, and then eleven, and then stopped counting. Three of them have been to exhibitions. The rest are in a drawer under the window in no order at all. He is seventy-six now and says he is not sure there will be a thirty-second, because his hands have begun to shake in the afternoon and the first week of January is in the afternoon.

title: 社区菜园里的三分地
material: The community garden has forty-one plots of three metres by two. Auntie Fu has plot number nineteen, and she counts everything, because two plots near her were taken by people who never came and one of those is now full of weeds nobody will clear. Her own plot has never had a weed in it. She grows greens, beans, two rows of spring onions and one squash, and the squash is the only thing she does not eat herself; it goes to the table in the yard on the last Sunday of the month. Watering is by a rota of eight people, three in the morning and one in the evening, in summer. Auntie Fu is always in the evening group and has never once been late, and the rota is on a board by the tap. The gate is shut at six and opened again at seven in the morning, and the key hangs on the second nail. Two years ago she offered her plot to a family from the next street and the family never came; she kept it and has never offered again. She says three metres by two is enough for four people if nobody plants potatoes.

title: 在阳台上养蚕的男生
material: Yu Tian keeps silkworms on a balcony on the eleventh floor, and last spring he took four hundred of them out of a paper bag his uncle had brought from the country. A tray is ten boxes, a box holds about thirty, and a tray therefore feeds about three hundred. He started with two trays, which was one too many, and by the last week he had three trays and half a bag of leaves left over. He feeds them at seven in the morning and at seven in the evening, and he says the evening feed is the one they wait for. The cocoons are made on a frame of dry twigs and are ready after about nine days. He keeps the best twenty for the moth case and gives the rest to the school, which will not feed them but will let the children look. In the autumn the moths come out, lay on paper, and die within three days. He has kept every paper. Nothing in the flat is used for anything else now.

title: 在候车亭画画的女孩
material: Ke Yan paints at the bus shelter at the end of the road on Saturday and Sunday afternoons, and the shelter is nine metres long, which gives her room for a stool, a box of water and a board. She is nineteen and has been doing it for three years. She does the same view: the road, the wall behind it and the two poles. What changes is the weather, and she has done that view in rain, in fog and in a heat that made the paint dry on the board before she could use it. She sells nothing and takes a hat, not a box for money. People stop; about eight of them say something and the rest look and go, and she has never once found that rude. The wall behind the view is scheduled to be painted over in the spring, and the council has not decided what colour. She says she will do the new wall too, and that the view will be the same, and that this is not a reason to stop. Her teacher thinks she should go to art college. She has not decided and she has until the spring.

title: 社区与邻里
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你所在社区的邻里关系，说说大家平时怎样互相帮忙。
modelAnswer: I live in a small community in Suzhou, where most of the buildings are no more than six floors high. The neighbours on our floor often talk to each other on the stairs, and they know almost every family on the floor. Old Mrs. Xu at number 12 keeps a small garden, and she gives tomatoes to anyone who knocks at her door. When my mother was ill last winter, three different families brought soup to our flat in the same week. One of them was the young couple upstairs, who had just moved in and hardly knew anyone. In summer we often share cold drinks on the steps after dinner. Last year our building collected rubbish together, because a new recycling point was opened at the corner. I think a good community depends on small acts rather than on big plans, and ours has plenty of them.

October and November are also the best months for walking, because the wind is cool and gentle. I usually take photographs of the same corner on every sunny weekend. In winter my hands hurt in the morning, and I have to wear three pairs of socks. Spring brings too many showers for me, since I often forget to carry an umbrella. Summer is the season I like least, because the rooms in my flat become hard to sleep in. Even so, the autumn holidays are when I feel happiest all year.

I also try to stay away from the phone for the first hour after I wake up. Sleep, water and movement are the three things I would keep if I could change nothing else.

title: 金钱与消费
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你买东西时的习惯，说说家里的钱主要花在哪里。
modelAnswer: Before I buy anything, I always write it on a list, and I put the list in my pocket when I go out. I rarely buy the first thing I see in the shop window, because a decision made in five seconds is usually a bad one. When a pair of shoes is reduced by half, I ask myself whether I really need a second pair. My family's biggest expense is my school fees, which take a large part of my father's income every year. The second biggest is food, and my mother buys most of it at the market near the station. I keep most of my own pocket money in a box at home, and I have never used a card for a small purchase. My uncle once told me that the people who spend carefully are not mean, they are simply clear about what matters. I have started to keep a small record, and it turns out that I save more than I thought.

title: 宠物与动物
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你和动物相处的经历，说说动物给你的生活带来了什么。
modelAnswer: We had a dog when I was nine, and he was a thin brown one that my father found beside the road. He followed my bicycle to school every day for six years, and he was always waiting at the gate when I came back. He died in the autumn of my first year in middle school, and our street was strangely quiet for months afterwards. Since then we have kept a small bowl of food on the wall for the cats behind the buildings. They appear only after dark, and none of them has a name that we know. Last winter a cat with one ear stopped coming, and we could only guess where it had gone. I believe animals measure time better than we do, because they do not count the years at all. A street with animals in it feels different from one without them, and I cannot explain exactly how.

信息完整性：猫只在天黑后出现、冬天断耳猫不再出现、狗去世后街道安静了几个月、动物对时间的感觉与人不同、有动物的街道感觉与没有的不同

title: 交通与出行
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你平时怎样上下学，说说现在的出行方式给你带来了什么。
modelAnswer: I go to school by bike, and the ride takes about fifteen minutes from my flat to the school gate. My father used to take me by car, but he stopped when I was in Grade Seven, because he said the streets are worse in the morning. There used to be a bus stop at the end of our road, and it was taken away two winters ago. Now I share the bike ride with my neighbour, whose children go to the same school. The new route takes a little longer, but the air on the way is much cleaner. In the rain we both wait under the awning of a shop until it eases. Traffic in our district is much lighter than it was five years ago, although the ring road is still slow at eight o'clock. My knees have never hurt, and I think that has more to do with the bicycle than with anything else.

title: 穿着与风格
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你平时怎样挑选衣服，说说你在穿着上的原则。
modelAnswer: I own very few clothes, and most of them were bought in the same shop near my home. My sister calls my style plain, and she is not wrong about that. I do not follow fashion because the things I like rarely change from one year to the next. What matters to me is whether a piece of clothes lasts, not whether it looks special this week. My mother taught me to check the label before anything, and I have thrown away three jackets since she said it. Uniforms make the mornings easier, since nobody at school notices that two girls wore the same blue shirt. I once bought a white pair of shoes for a school trip, and they were ruined by the second afternoon. Now I keep one dark pair for everything, and I have stopped worrying about what other people are wearing.

title: 音乐与艺术
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你接触过的艺术形式，说说你最喜欢的是什么。
modelAnswer: The first music I noticed was in my grandmother's house, where an old radio sat on a high shelf and was never switched off. I still remember a song that she hummed while she cooked, and I have never found out what it was called. My cousin taught me to play the erhu when I was twelve, and I was terrible at it for a full year. Watercolours came later, at a club that met on Friday afternoons, and they taught me to look at ordinary things more slowly. Painting has one advantage over music: a bad picture is still worth showing. Music has one advantage over painting: it can follow you along the street for free. Music is what I like most of the three, because it follows me down the street for free and it never asks for an exam result. My grandmother could not read the radio dial, and she never needed to.

title: 科技与手机
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈手机在你生活里的位置，说说它带来方便的同时带来了什么。
modelAnswer: My phone is the first thing I touch when I wake up, and the last thing I look at before I sleep, which my mother does not enjoy hearing. It replaces almost everything else in my bag: a dictionary, a map, a notebook, a ticket and a wallet. When I travel, the paper tickets it used to be are the only thing I still carry. I know where the bus goes without waiting for a sign, and I know the way home in three towns I have never studied. The cost is harder to measure, because I do not lose an hour a day deliberately; it simply disappears. Last term I stopped taking it into the dormitory on Sunday nights, and I read two books that I would otherwise have scrolled past. My phone has never once let me get lost, and that is not a small thing. I would not give it up, but I would like to be a person who can put it face down for an hour.

title: 规则与公共秩序
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈公共场合需要守的规矩，说说规矩为什么必要。
modelAnswer: On the bus, everybody queues even when there are only three people waiting, and nobody pushes, which would be unthinkable in some other cities. In the library we keep our voices low enough that the person next to us can hear themselves think. When someone drops something, the rule is simple: you stop, you pick it up, and you carry it back to them yourself. Most public rules were written by somebody who had a problem once, and I have found out that this is almost always true. My own school banned phones from the dining hall last year, and the first week was full of complaints. By the second week the hall was so quiet that we could hear the clock. Somebody has to decide these things, and it is easier to decide them once than to argue about them every day. A rule is not there to stop you from doing anything; it is there so that the people around you are not paying for your convenience.

title: 友谊与合作
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈和朋友合作做的事情，说说合作教会了你什么。
modelAnswer: Our class spent a whole term building a model bridge out of paper, and the four of us divided the work in a way that nobody had planned. I drew the shape, my friend cut the pieces, and two others held everything together with glue they were not supposed to use. On the last afternoon the bridge held more weight than the teacher had expected, and we all knew exactly which part of it would fail first. What I learned was less about bridges than about patience. When a plan is agreed quickly, somebody's idea disappears quietly, and you only notice when the work is finished. My friend and I still argue about small things, and we have never once walked away from a job half done. We still meet the four of us once a year, and we rebuild something small each time. Cooperation is slower than doing something alone, and afterwards it belongs to more than one person.

title: 失败与挫折
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈一次你没有做成的事情，说说你从那次结果里得到了什么。
modelAnswer: Last year I entered an English speech competition, and I finished fourth out of eleven, which was not the result I had repeated in my head for weeks. I had memorised my speech word for word, and when the lights went on I forgot the second paragraph entirely. Afterwards three classmates told me it had been a good speech, and I did not believe any of them. What helped was writing it down afterwards, line by line, and seeing that my pauses were the problem rather than my English. This term I entered again, and I used short notes instead of a full script. I came third, and the difference between the two years was about six pages of paper. I showed that speech to my cousin afterwards, and she said it was better than I thought. Failing once is cheap if you read the result properly, and expensive only if you decide it was about your worth.

title: 未来与变化
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你希望将来的生活有什么变化，说说你打算为此做什么。
modelAnswer: Ten years from now I hope to live in a smaller flat than this one, but not far from where my parents will be living. I would like to work in a place where I can see the sky from my desk, and I am aware that this narrows my choices. The change I care about most has nothing to do with money, although money makes it easier. I want to be able to switch off my phone at the end of a working day and not feel that something is being missed. My father did that for years, and he has never once told me it was easy. The first step is small: I am learning to cook, because feeding myself is a skill nobody can take away when the price of a restaurant goes up. My mother thinks the plan is reasonable, which is more than I expected. Plans like this are easy to write down and hard to keep, so I have told my sister to ask me about it every month.

title: 志愿服务与社区

modelAnswer: Last summer I joined a volunteer team in my neighbourhood. Every Saturday morning we cleaned the small park near my flat, and two old men always thanked us at the gate. Our team gave away free books at the gate of a primary school last term. I also visited a home for the elderly once a month and talked with the old people there. I was a little afraid at first, because I did not know what to say to them. They asked me many questions about my school, and I learned that listening is more useful than talking. We collected old books for a village school in the countryside. Collecting them took two weekends. This year I want to teach English to children on Sunday afternoons.

title: 阅读与书

modelAnswer: Last National Day my family went to a small town near Lake Tai by train. We left Suzhou at seven in the morning and arrived two hours later. title: 友谊与同学

title: 家乡变化

modelAnswer: My hometown is a small city near Suzhou, and it has changed a lot in recent years. Five years ago the road near my home was narrow and full of dust. Now it is wide and there are green trees on both sides. A new library was built behind my school last year. Before it opened, many students had nowhere to study quietly. I love the old streets, but I also want a better city for the people who live there.

title: 传统文化
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你感兴趣的中国传统文化，谈谈它为什么值得保留。
modelAnswer: I am interested in Chinese paper cutting, and my grandmother can do it very well. She learned it when she was young, fifty years ago. Every Spring Festival she puts red paper animals on the windows of our flat. The only tools she needs are a pair of scissors and one sheet of paper. Children in our building always stop to watch her hands. Paper cutting has no words at all, and yet it can tell a whole story. My school once held a small show about it. Other people may think it is old-fashioned, but I believe it belongs to everyone.

title: 科技与生活
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，说说你最常用的科技工具，谈谈它改变了你生活的哪一点。
modelAnswer: The tool I use most is my phone, and I would be lost without it. I pay for things, take photos, and check my timetable with it every day. My father often asks me to look up a bus time for him. I also check the weather on it before I go out. The change I like most is that I no longer need to carry a paper dictionary. title: 时间管理与计划
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你安排学习时间的方式，谈谈计划对你有没有帮助。
modelAnswer: I make a short plan for every evening before dinner. I write my homework on a small card and put it on my desk. The hardest subject always comes first, because I am still fresh at that time. My desk is beside the window, so the card is easy to see. When I finish a subject I put the card back in my bag. If I finish it early, I review my mistakes for half an hour. A plan is not a promise, so I also leave ten minutes for a break. Last month my marks went up, and I finally stopped feeling nervous before an exam.

title: 压力与心情
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你遇到压力时的反应，谈谈什么办法对你最有效。
modelAnswer: Before an exam I sometimes feel so nervous that I cannot sleep. I try to tell myself that one paper does not decide everything. Last year I made myself a list of everything I was afraid of, and reading it made the problem smaller. My best friend told me to talk to our teacher, which felt hard at first. I also tried running slowly for twenty minutes, and it worked better than I expected. Now I write three lines about my feelings before every test. My mother says I look calmer now. Doing that really helps me sleep well the night before.

title: 未来与理想
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，谈谈你将来想做什么，谈谈现在的你为此做了哪些准备。
modelAnswer: In the future I want to be a doctor, because I care about people when they are ill. My grandmother was ill last winter, and the way the doctors spoke to us was calm and kind. So far I have only studied hard at school, and that is not enough. Every weekend I read one book about medicine, which is difficult but useful. I also join school science talks to learn how a real hospital works. My classmates think doctors have long working hours, and they are right. My teacher says medicine needs patience as well as science. I know this road is long, and I am ready to walk it.

prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你的个人信息与一项爱好，说清楚它对你意味着什么。
modelAnswer: My name is Li Wei and I am fifteen years old. I study in a middle school in Suzhou, and I am in Grade Nine this year. I am not very tall, but I am good at running. My favourite subject is history, because our teacher tells stories about real people. I play the guitar after dinner almost every evening, and I practise for about half an hour. I also like drawing, although I am not good at it yet. Last year I won a small prize in a school drawing competition. In my free time I help my grandmother water her flowers on the balcony. prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你的校园生活，说说你最喜欢其中哪一部分。
modelAnswer: Our school is not very big, but it has a new library and a big playground. Classes begin at eight in the morning and finish at half past four in the afternoon. We have six lessons a day, and the longest break is the one after lunch. My favourite teacher is our maths teacher, because she never hurries us when we make a mistake. Our school has three clubs, and I am in the reading club. We meet every Friday afternoon and talk about one book together. Sometimes we also play basketball on the playground after school. modelAnswer: I live with my parents and my younger sister in a flat near the city centre. My father is a driver and he often works on weekends, so we usually have dinner together only on weekdays. On Sundays we often visit my grandparents in a small town near Suzhou. My grandmother always cooks us fish, and my grandfather likes telling stories about his childhood. modelAnswer: Last summer I went to Hangzhou with my parents, and we stayed there for five days. We took a high-speed train, and the journey took about two hours. We also visited a tea plantation in the afternoon of that day. I liked the trip because it was the first time I had travelled by train. modelAnswer: I have played badminton for about three years, and I usually play it with my classmates after school. We go to the sports hall twice a week, and each time we play for about an hour. I am not very fast, but I can keep going for a long time. Our school sports meeting is in October, and I have signed up for the eight-hundred-metre race. title: 饮食

modelAnswer: Our family does not eat much meat, so we have vegetables almost every day. For breakfast I usually have an egg, some bread and a glass of milk. title: 节日

modelAnswer: The Spring Festival is the most important festival in China, and my family always celebrates it together. Before the festival we clean the house and put up red couplets on the door. On New Year's Eve we have a big dinner, and my grandmother makes dumplings. After dinner we watch a programme on television until midnight. Last year my cousin gave me a red envelope, and I saved most of the money for a book. I also like the Mid-Autumn Festival, because we eat mooncakes and sit outside together. modelAnswer: I live in Suzhou, which is a city with many gardens and old streets. The air here is much better than it was ten years ago, because the factories have moved away. People in my neighbourhood take their rubbish to the recycling point instead of putting it in the river. My family walks or takes the bus instead of driving when we go to the city centre. modelAnswer: I read a lot, but these days most of my reading is done on my phone. I usually read English news after dinner, and it takes me about twenty minutes. modelAnswer: I want to be a teacher when I grow up, although my parents hope that I will study science. title: 校园规则
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍学校里的规则，说说你最看重哪条规则。
modelAnswer: Our school has about six rules that every student must follow. We must wear the school uniform from Monday to Friday, and we are not allowed to wear jeans. We cannot use our phones in class, although we may keep them in our bags. Mobile phones must be handed to the teacher before a test. I think the rule about phones is the most useful one, because a phone on a desk takes our attention away. Last year our class broke this rule twice in one week, and the teacher was angry. After that our class made a rule of our own: we put every phone in a box at the door. The school also has a rule about running in the stairs, and nobody is allowed to run there. I agree with that one as well, because people get hurt in staircases.

title: 出行与交通工具
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你上学使用的交通方式，说说这种出行方式给你带来的变化。
modelAnswer: I go to school by bike every day, and the ride takes about fifteen minutes. My father bought me an old bike two years ago, and he fixed the brakes himself. In the past I took a bus, and the queue at the stop made me late nearly every morning. Last winter I started to ride in heavy rain, which was cold but also healthy. Now I leave home ten minutes earlier, and I am never late for the first class. Riding has changed my body as well, because I feel stronger in my legs. It has also made me more careful when I cross a big road. My father says that I should wear a bright jacket at night, and now I always carry a small light on my bag. I hope I can keep riding when I go to high school next year.

title: 音乐与艺术
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你喜欢的那种艺术形式，说说它怎样影响了你。
modelAnswer: The art form I like best is black-and-white photography. My father showed me how to use his old camera when I was in Grade Eight. Photography is different from painting, because a camera does not let you add anything afterwards. I keep a small notebook with the ideas for every shoot. Last spring I photographed my grandmother in her kitchen, and she laughed because she had not seen herself in twenty years. That photograph now hangs above my desk. Photography has made me more careful about light, and I notice shadows in the street now. It has also taught me to be patient, since a good picture often needs thirty minutes. My mother says I look at the world more slowly since I started. I hope to bring a real camera on our next trip.

title: 健康习惯
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你保持健康时坚持的习惯，说说坚持之后你身上出现了什么变化。
modelAnswer: The habit I keep is drinking warm water when I get up. I started it last September because I often had a sore throat in the morning. My grandfather told me that warm water is better for us than cold water in winter. Now I drink two glasses before breakfast, and then I do twenty deep breaths by the window. This habit is small, but it has changed my mornings. I used to skip breakfast, and now I eat an apple first. After three months I hardly catch a cold. My mother says my skin is better than last year, and I believe her. My classmate Li Na began the same habit in October, and she also feels fine now. I hope I can keep it for many years, because health is more useful than marks.

title: 科技与生活
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍改变了你生活的科技产品，说说它给你带来的好处与麻烦。
modelAnswer: The product that changed my life most is my phone, which I got for my birthday two years ago. Before that I used a small keypad phone for calls only. Now I keep my timetable, my dictionary and my notes in it, so I do not need a paper notebook. The biggest advantage is that I can check a word in two seconds. Another advantage is that my parents can call me when I walk home. However, there is a problem as well. When I look at short videos, I lose twenty minutes without noticing. My father told me to keep the phone in another room when I study, and now I do that every evening. In this way the phone helps me and hurts me at the same time. I think a person should choose how to use it, not the other way round.

title: 动物与宠物

modelAnswer: The animal I like best is the dog, and my family has kept one for six years. His name is Doudou, and he is a brown dog with white feet. Doudou waits at the gate every afternoon, so he knows the sound of my steps. My father chose him from a litter next door, and my mother feeds him when she is at home. He never runs into the road, because my father trained him when he was young. Dogs show their feelings more openly than people do, and Doudou is never unhappy for long. From him I learned that a calm animal is easier to live with. I also learned that animals need a fixed routine, so I keep my own study time every evening. Our neighbour has a cat, and the two of them meet at the gate every weekend. Next year I hope to learn how to train a puppy, because Doudou is getting old.

prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你学会的花钱方式，说说它怎样帮你攒下了钱。
modelAnswer: The way I learned to spend money is to put my pocket money into three jars. My mother gave me an old coffee jar, and I bought two cheap ones at a shop near my home. One jar is for books, one is for snacks with my friends, and the last one is for things I want but do not need. At the end of each month I count the money in the last jar. title: 家乡的变化
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你的家乡，说说近些年它发生了哪些变化。
modelAnswer: My hometown is a small town near Suzhou, and about three thousand people live there. Ten years ago the main street had only a shop and a post office. Today the same street has a supermarket, a bookshop and two coffee places. The biggest change is the bus line, because it now comes every ten minutes instead of twice an hour. Another change is the park beside the river, which was a piece of waste ground before. Old houses were pulled down, and the new ones are taller, so the town looks quite different now. My grandparents miss the old market, but my mother likes the new supermarket. The town is still small, yet it is much easier to live in than before. title: 挫折与坚持
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍一件你原来做不好的事，说说你后来怎么改进的。
modelAnswer: The thing I could not do well was public speaking. In Grade Seven I was asked to read a poem to the whole class, and my hands shook so much that I dropped the paper. I sat down without finishing and said nothing. A year later I joined the debate club, because my English teacher said that talking is a skill like riding a bike. The first month was hard, and I spoke in short sentences only. I practised reading aloud for ten minutes every evening and recorded myself on my phone. In the spring I took part in a school speech contest and won third prize. That was not a big prize, but it meant more than the first prize in Grade Six. The change did not come from talent, and it came from practice. I still get nervous before I speak, but now I keep talking anyway.

title: 网络安全
prompt: 请用英语作一段话，介绍你在网上保护个人信息时遵守的做法。
modelAnswer: The rule I follow online is simple: I never put my real name on a public page. When I joined a fan forum last year, I used a nickname instead. I also never send photos of my school uniform with the school name on it. My cousin once posted such a photo, and a stranger found his class. That frightened us both, so we deleted it on the same evening. I check the padlock at the top of every page before I type anything, and I close the window when I use a public computer at school. My passwords are never the same twice, and I keep them in a notebook at home. These habits are not difficult, although I forget them when I am tired. I think online safety is a skill, and skills improve with practice.
